newsitem.title: GERMANY: German pay deal sparks hopes over dispute.
newsitem.headline: German pay deal sparks hopes over dispute.

text.p: A surprise decision by metal and engineering employers in the German state of Lower Saxony not to enforce a law cutting sick pay sparked hopes on Thursday of a wider settlement that could avert threatened strikes.

Negotiators said that after 13 hours of talks in the northern town of Hanover they had agreed a package maintaining sick pay at 100 percent of salary, spurning an unpopular new law allowing employers to cut sick pay to 80 percent.
"The accord is a breakthrough in the metal industry," Juergen Peters, chief negotiator for the IG Metall trade union said on Thursday.
The law was introduced by Chancellor Helmut Kohl's government in October as part of wide-ranging austerity measures aimed at securing German entry to European economic and monetary union in 1999.

While Peters stressed the deal was only applicable to the 90,000 metal and engineering workers in Lower Saxony, union officials said they were now more optimistic that similar agreements could be reached elsewhere in the industry.
"When employers participate as they did in Lower Saxony, there will be deals in other regions -- that is my hope at least," an IG Metall spokeswoman said in Frankfurt.
Opposition leaders reacted with glee to the decision by employers not to adopt the new law on sick pay, calling it a slap in the face for Kohl's government.

"The Bonn coalition, the destroyer of social peace, should sit up and take notice of the sense of responsibility shown (by the two sides)," Rudolf Scharping, parliamentary leader of the opposition Social Democrats (SPD), said in a statement.
All-out strikes in the sector, where stoppages have already cost firms such as carmaker Mercedes Benz millions of marks, had been seen as increasingly likely next spring.

Employer representatives, while noticeably less enthusiastic about the deal than their union counterparts, said the full package would, for the average firm in the sector, mean a cost increase of less than one percent next year.

"Regional employer federations will in the next weeks decide whether they want to take on the Hanover agreement," the Gesamtmetall metal and engineering employers group said in a statement. ($1=1.5608 Mark)
